orig_9709_p3_vec_components.description: Use 2D and 3D vectors to describe position, displacement, length and midpoint.

sections.title: How do I read a vector in 2D or 3D?
sections.label: Read the notation
sections.intro: An ordered list of components describes a movement. The point \(P(2,-1,3)\) has position vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}\). The same column can describe a displacement between other points.

blocks.html: Unit vectors \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) point along the positive axes. In 2D use two components. In 3D use three, including a zero for any direction with no movement.
Keep the coordinate order when switching forms. In \(2\mathbf i-3\mathbf k\), the second component is zero.

blocks.title: Read the basis components
blocks.prompt: Write \(- 2 \mathbf i - 4 \mathbf j\) as a column vector. Give all 3 components.
blocks.hint: An omitted basis direction has coefficient zero. Keep the column in coordinate order.
blocks.solution:
The coefficients of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) give the components in that order.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: Which point do I subtract first?
sections.label: Subtract positions
sections.intro: Think of a route from the origin. Going to \(A\) and then moving by \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) must arrive at \(B\). Reversing the route negates the displacement.

blocks.html: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\). The arrow reads start to finish, while the subtraction reads finish minus start.

figure.alt: Three arrows show the route from O to A, from O to B and from A to B.
figure.caption: The route \(O\to A\to B\) and the direct route \(O\to B\) have the same total displacement.

blocks.html: Subtracting \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) from \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) gives \(\overrightarrow{BA}\). A distance check alone cannot spot this reversal.

blocks.title: Find endpoint minus start point
blocks.prompt: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for \(A(-5, 2, 4)\) and \(B(3, -1, -2)\).

retry.feedback: That is the first component of the return displacement. Subtract the position of A from the position of B.

blocks.hint: Write the endpoint above the start point before subtracting.
blocks.solution:
The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\-3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: How do I add and scale movements?
sections.label: Add and scale
sections.intro: To take two steps, translate the second arrow so it starts at the first arrow’s tip. To multiply by a scalar, multiply all the components by that number.

blocks.html: The parallelogram diagonal is the sum of the adjacent side vectors. A negative scalar reverses direction as it changes length.
Scaling one component alone generally changes the direction, so it does not give a parallel vector.

blocks.title: Complete a parallelogram
blocks.prompt: \(DABC\) is a parallelogram, with vertices given in order. Find \(B\) if \(D(2, 1, -1)\), \(A(5, 4, 0)\) and \(C(0, 3, 4)\). Give all coordinates.
blocks.hint: Use the displacement from D to C, then start that movement at A.
blocks.solution:
Opposite edges have the same directed displacement, so \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}\).

Add the displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) to the position of \(A\).

The resulting point is \(B(3, 6, 5)\).

sections.title: How do I find length and unit direction?
sections.label: Measure and normalise
sections.intro: Use Pythagoras on mutually perpendicular axes. The length is \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\) in 3D. In 2D omit the last term. A direction without its original speed or length can be given by a unit vector.

blocks.html: For non-zero \(\mathbf d\), the unit vector along it is \(\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\). For the opposite unit vector, use \(-\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\).
The zero vector has length zero and no direction. Dividing it by its length does not define a unit vector.
Check the exact unit vector by squaring its three components and adding. The sum should be \(1\).

blocks.title: Build a unit vector
blocks.prompt: Find the length of \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and the unit vector opposite to \(\mathbf d\). Give exact entries.

retry.feedback: That vector points in the original direction. Reverse all components for the requested direction.

blocks.hint: Use the square root of the sum of the squares, and keep track of the requested direction.
blocks.solution:
Pythagoras gives \(|\mathbf d|=6\).

Reverse the signs, then divide all components by the positive length.

The length is \(6\) and the requested unit vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{3}\\- \frac{2}{3}\\- \frac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: Why does averaging locate the midpoint?
sections.label: Find a midpoint
sections.intro: Start at \(A\) and take half the displacement to \(B\). This gives an average of the endpoint position vectors, and it works in either dimension.

blocks.html: \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB})\).
Half of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is a displacement from \(A\), not usually a position from \(O\).

blocks.title: Find the midpoint
blocks.prompt: Find the midpoint of \(AB\) when \(A(2, 9, -6)\) and \(B(-5, 1, 8)\). Give all coordinates.
blocks.hint: Average the position vectors. Half the displacement alone starts at the wrong place.
blocks.solution:
At the midpoint the displacement from \(A\) is half of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).

Average the two position vectors. \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac12\left(\begin{pmatrix}2\\9\\-6\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\8\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{3}{2}\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

The midpoint is \(M(- \frac{3}{2}, 5, 1)\).

glossary.definition: The displacement from the origin to a point.
An ordered movement from a specified start to a specified endpoint.

examples.title: Read the basis components
examples.question: Write \(3 \mathbf i - 5 \mathbf k\) as a column vector. Give all 3 components.
solution: The coefficients of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) give the components in that order.
The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-5\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find endpoint minus start point
examples.question: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for \(A(2, -3, 5)\) and \(B(-4, 1, 2)\).
solution: The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find endpoint minus start point
examples.question: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for \(A(6, -3)\) and \(B(-2, 0)\).
solution: The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Combine two vectors
examples.question: Given \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}\), calculate \(2 \mathbf a - 3 \mathbf b\). Give all components.
solution: Scale every component before adding or subtracting.
\(2 \mathbf a - 3 \mathbf b=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}-3\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\8\\-19\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Complete a parallelogram
examples.question: \(DABC\) is a parallelogram, with vertices given in order. Find \(B\) if \(D(3, -2, 2)\), \(A(4, 3, 0)\) and \(C(-1, 0, 5)\). Give all coordinates.
solution: Opposite edges have the same directed displacement, so \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}\).
Add the displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\) to the position of \(A\).
The resulting point is \(B(0, 5, 3)\).

examples.title: Build a unit vector
examples.question: Find the length of \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\6\end{pmatrix}\) and the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf d\). Give exact entries.
solution: Pythagoras gives \(|\mathbf d|=7\).
Divide every component by the positive length, preserving their signs.
The length is \(7\) and the requested unit vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{7}\\- \frac{3}{7}\\\frac{6}{7}\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find the midpoint
examples.question: Find the midpoint of \(AB\) when \(A(3, -8, 1)\) and \(B(-5, 2, 4)\). Give all coordinates.
solution: At the midpoint the displacement from \(A\) is half of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).

Average the two position vectors. \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac12\left(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-8\\1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-3\\\frac{5}{2}\end{pmatrix}\).
The midpoint is \(M(-1, -3, \frac{5}{2})\).

revision.checks:

  • Preserve a zero component when switching forms.
  • A unit vector has a squared length of one.
revision.examTip: Show the exact magnitude before normalising. A negative component records direction.

extraPractice.title: Read the basis components
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(6 \mathbf i - 5 \mathbf j\) as a column vector. Give all 3 components.
extraPractice.hint: An omitted basis direction has coefficient zero. Keep the column in coordinate order.
extraPractice.solution:
The coefficients of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) give the components in that order.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-5\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

extraPractice.title: Find endpoint minus start point
extraPractice.prompt: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and the exact length \(AB\) for \(A(3, -6, 2)\) and \(B(-2, 1, 4)\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the endpoint above the start point before subtracting.
extraPractice.solution:
The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\7\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

The displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\7\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(AB=\sqrt{78}\), found by squaring and adding the components before taking the square root.

extraPractice.title: Combine two vectors
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\7\\3\end{pmatrix}\), calculate \(- \mathbf a + 2 \mathbf b\). Give all components.
extraPractice.hint: Apply each coefficient to its whole vector before combining like components.
extraPractice.solution:
Scale every component before adding or subtracting.

\(- \mathbf a + 2 \mathbf b=-\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}+2\begin{pmatrix}-4\\7\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-10\\14\\9\end{pmatrix}\).

extraPractice.title: Build a unit vector
extraPractice.prompt: Find the length of \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf d\). Give exact entries.
extraPractice.hint: Use the square root of the sum of the squares, and keep track of the requested direction.
extraPractice.solution:
Pythagoras gives \(|\mathbf d|=7\).

Divide every component by the positive length, preserving their signs.

The length is \(7\) and the requested unit vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{6}{7}\\- \frac{3}{7}\\\frac{2}{7}\end{pmatrix}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the midpoint
extraPractice.prompt: Find the midpoint of \(AB\) when \(A(2, 2)\) and \(B(5, -3)\). Give all coordinates.
extraPractice.hint: Average the position vectors. Half the displacement alone starts at the wrong place.
extraPractice.solution:
At the midpoint the displacement from \(A\) is half of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).

Average the two position vectors. \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac12\left(\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{7}{2}\\- \frac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\).

The midpoint is \(M(\frac{7}{2}, - \frac{1}{2})\).

orig_9709_p3_vec_line_equations.description: Build line equations from points and directions, test membership and restrict parameters to a segment.

sections.title: What does each part of a line equation do?
sections.label: Read the line
sections.intro: In \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\), \(\mathbf a\) fixes the position at \(t=0\), and non-zero \(\mathbf d\) gives the direction of movement as \(t\) increases.

blocks.html: The position vector \(\mathbf r\) changes with \(t\). A whole straight line uses all real values of \(t\), including negative values.

figure.alt: A rising straight line has points marked in order P, A, B. Its direction arrow points from A towards B.
figure.caption: At \(t=0\) the vector line is at its anchor \(A\). Increasing \(t\) moves along the direction arrow.

blocks.html: A negative parameter moves in the opposite sense from the direction arrow. The direction vector does not have to have length one.

blocks.title: Read a point from its parameter
blocks.prompt: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\5\\-1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=\frac{3}{2}\). Give all coordinates.

retry.feedback: That uses the negative parameter. The question gives a positive value of t.

blocks.hint: Multiply the direction vector by the parameter, then add the anchor.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\5\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{9}{2}\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

The point is \(P(\frac{9}{2}, 2, 5)\).

sections.title: How do two points determine a line?
sections.label: Build the line
sections.intro: Either point can anchor the line. Take the difference of the two position vectors to get a direction. Swapping their order reverses the arrow along the same line.

blocks.html: For distinct points \(A\) and \(B\), one form is \(\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+t\overrightarrow{AB}\). In this form, \(t=0\) gives \(A\) and \(t=1\) gives \(B\).
Using a second position vector as the direction only works in special cases. Start with endpoint minus start point.

blocks.title: Write a line through two points
blocks.prompt: Use \(A(-1, 3, 8)\) and \(B(-1, -1, 14)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(B\) and use \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.
blocks.hint: An endpoint is a position. A direction is a difference of two positions.
blocks.solution:
Use the position of \(B\) for the anchor.

\(\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-6\end{pmatrix}\) by subtracting the starting position from the final one.

The line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\14\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: How do I test whether a point is on the line?
sections.label: Test membership
sections.intro: Write the three coordinate equations and use a changing coordinate to get a candidate parameter. All coordinates must agree at that same value.

blocks.html: In a fixed coordinate, the direction component is zero. That coordinate must equal the anchor coordinate at every point of the line.
Separate values of \(t\) for different coordinates never establish membership.

blocks.title: Check all coordinates
blocks.prompt: Does \(P(3, 9, -1)\) lie on \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\)?

retry.feedback: The y-coordinate determines the parameter, but the first coordinate is fixed at 2 and the candidate point has first coordinate 3.

blocks.hint: Fit one changing coordinate first. A mismatch elsewhere rules out membership.
blocks.solution:
The y-coordinate forces \(t=1\).

At this value the position on the line is \((2, 9, -1)\), but \(P=(3, 9, -1)\).

No. A single parameter must give every coordinate of the point.

sections.title: Can the same line have a different equation?
sections.label: Reparameterise
sections.intro: Choose another anchor already on the line, and scale the direction by a non-zero number. The new parameter still traces all the same points.

blocks.html: If \(\mathbf b=\mathbf a+s\mathbf d\), then \(\mathbf b+u(c\mathbf d)\) equals \(\mathbf a+(s+cu)\mathbf d\). With \(c\ne0\), the parameter \(s+cu\) ranges over every real number.
A parallel direction alone does not establish that two equations describe the same line. The anchor must be on the original line.

blocks.title: Change the anchor and direction
blocks.prompt: A line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Rewrite it using the point at \(t=-1\) as the new anchor and \(3\mathbf d\) as the direction, where \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Give both vectors.
blocks.hint: Changing the parameter origin can change the anchor. Scale the full direction vector.
blocks.solution:
The new anchor is \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}+\left(-1\right)\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

Multiplying a direction by a non-zero scalar changes the parameter scale or sense. It covers the same set of points.

One equivalent form is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-9\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: How do I identify points on the segment AB?
sections.label: Restrict a segment
sections.intro: The entire line through \(A\) and \(B\) also extends beyond its endpoints. In the parameterisation from \(A\) along the full displacement \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), the endpoints are \(t=0\) and \(t=1\).

blocks.html: \(0\le t\le1\) describes the closed segment for this particular choice of anchor and direction. At \(t=\tfrac12\), the point is the midpoint.
With a different direction scale, the parameter of \(B\) may no longer be \(1\). Find it before restricting the parameter.

blocks.title: Read a point from its parameter
blocks.prompt: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\7\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\\8\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=\frac{3}{4}\). Give all coordinates.
blocks.hint: Multiply the direction vector by the parameter, then add the anchor.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\7\end{pmatrix}+\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\\8\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-2\\13\end{pmatrix}\).

The point is \(P(6, -2, 13)\).

glossary.definition: The point represented when the line parameter is zero.
A non-zero displacement parallel to the line.
A real number that picks a position on the line.
The part of a line between two given endpoints, including the endpoints here.

examples.title: Read a point from its parameter
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=-2\). Give all coordinates.
solution: Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.
\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\left(-2\right)\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Write a line through two points
examples.question: Use \(A(2, 1, -4)\) and \(B(6, -5, -2)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(A\) and use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.
solution: Use the position of \(A\) for the anchor.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\) by subtracting the starting position from the final one.
The line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Write a line through two points
examples.question: Use \(A(1, 6)\) and \(B(-5, 8)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(A\) and use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.
solution: Use the position of \(A\) for the anchor.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\) by subtracting the starting position from the final one.
The line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Test point membership
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\\7\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the parameter of \(P(0, -8, 13)\) and verify the other coordinates.
solution: The y-coordinate requires \(2 t - 4=-8\), so \(t=-2\).
Test the same value in the full equation. It gives \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\-8\\13\end{pmatrix}\), which matches all the coordinates.
The point lies on the line at \(t=-2\).

examples.title: Test point membership
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Find the parameter of \(P(3, 5, 4)\) and verify the other coordinates.
solution: The x-coordinate requires \(2 t + 2=3\), so \(t=\frac{1}{2}\).
Test the same value in the full equation. It gives \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}\), which matches all the coordinates.
The point lies on the line at \(t=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Change the anchor and direction
examples.question: A line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Rewrite it using the point at \(t=2\) as the new anchor and \(-2\mathbf d\) as the direction, where \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Give both vectors.
solution: The new anchor is \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\\3\end{pmatrix}+\left(2\right)\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\).
Multiplying a direction by a non-zero scalar changes the parameter scale or sense. It covers the same set of points.
One equivalent form is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Read a point from its parameter
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-3\\9\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=\frac{1}{3}\). Give all coordinates.
solution: Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.
\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\begin{pmatrix}-3\\9\\6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\\6\end{pmatrix}\).
The point is \(P(5, 0, 6)\).

revision.examTip: When using two points, check that substituting the second endpoint gives its full position vector.

extraPractice.title: Read a point from its parameter
extraPractice.prompt: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=- \frac{3}{2}\). Give all coordinates.

The point is \(P(4, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2})\).

extraPractice.title: Write a line through two points
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(A(5, -1, 6)\) and \(B(4, -3, 10)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(A\) and use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.

extraPractice.title: Test point membership
extraPractice.prompt: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the parameter of \(P(8, -1, 7)\). Check the other coordinates in your working.
extraPractice.hint: Find a candidate parameter from a changing coordinate. Check every coordinate with that same value.
extraPractice.solution:
The x-coordinate requires \(4 t=8\), so \(t=2\).

Test the same value in the full equation. It gives \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\), which matches all the coordinates.

The point lies on the line at \(t=2\).

extraPractice.title: Change the anchor and direction
extraPractice.prompt: A line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Rewrite it using the point at \(t=2\) as the new anchor and \(-3\mathbf d\) as the direction, where \(\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Give both vectors.
extraPractice.hint: Changing the parameter origin can change the anchor. Scale the full direction vector.
extraPractice.solution:
The new anchor is \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\left(2\right)\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}9\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\).

Multiplying a direction by a non-zero scalar changes the parameter scale or sense. It covers the same set of points.

One equivalent form is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}9\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-9\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

extraPractice.title: Read a point from its parameter
extraPractice.prompt: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}6\\-9\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=\frac{1}{3}\). Give all coordinates.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the direction vector by the parameter, then add the anchor.
extraPractice.solution:
Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\6\end{pmatrix}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\begin{pmatrix}6\\-9\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

The point is \(P(4, 0, 5)\).

orig_9709_p3_vec_scalar_product.description: Use scalar products to find directed vector angles, smaller line angles and perpendicular directions.

sections.title: How do two vectors produce a single number?
sections.label: Use the dot product
sections.intro: Multiply matching components and add the products. The resulting scalar can be negative, zero or positive.

blocks.html: With \(\mathbf a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)\) and \(\mathbf b=(b_x,b_y,b_z)\) written as component triples, \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z\).
Elementwise products alone give three values. Add them to finish the dot product.

blocks.title: Find the scalar product
blocks.prompt: Calculate \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\) for \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: The result is one number. Preserve the sign of every product.
blocks.solution:
Multiply corresponding components, then add.

\(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\left(2\right)\left(7\right)+\left(-5\right)\left(4\right)+\left(1\right)\left(-2\right)=-8\).

sections.title: When does the angle between vectors become obtuse?
sections.label: Find a vector angle
sections.intro: Put both vector arrows tail to tail. For non-zero vectors, divide the dot product by the two positive magnitudes to get the cosine of their angle.

blocks.html: \(\cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}\), with \(0^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ\). A negative dot product gives an obtuse angle unless the arrows point in exactly opposite directions.
Do not remove a negative sign from the dot product when the question asks for the angle between directed vectors.

blocks.title: Find the angle between two vectors
blocks.prompt: Find the angle \(\theta\) between the vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\). Give the exact value of \(\cos\theta\).
blocks.hint: Divide the correct scalar product by the product of the magnitudes before taking the inverse cosine.
blocks.solution:
Keep the sign of the scalar product \(-3\) because the two vector arrows have fixed directions.

The magnitudes are \(\sqrt{14}\) and \(\sqrt{13}\), giving \(\cos\theta=- \frac{3 \sqrt{182}}{182}\).

\(\cos\theta=- \frac{3 \sqrt{182}}{182}\).

sections.title: Why can the sign change for a line angle?
sections.label: Find a line angle
sections.intro: A direction vector can be reversed without changing a line. The angle between two lines is the smaller angle made by a pair of their directions, whether or not the lines meet.

blocks.html: Use \(\cos\theta=\frac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}\) to get \(0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ\).

figure.alt: Two lines cross. Two solid direction arrows make an obtuse angle, while a dotted reverse arrow shows the smaller angle.
figure.caption: Either sense can describe the teal line. Its smaller angle with the blue line is the acute angle in this sketch.

blocks.html: The anchor points do not describe the inclinations of the lines. Use their direction vectors, and round the angle only at the end.

blocks.title: Find the smaller line angle
blocks.prompt: Find the smaller angle \(\theta\) between \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\3\end{pmatrix}\). Give your answer in degrees to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Divide the correct scalar product by the product of the magnitudes before taking the inverse cosine.
blocks.solution:
Use the direction vectors. Their dot product is \(-4\). The absolute value gives the smaller angle because either direction can represent a line.

The magnitudes are \(3\) and \(\sqrt{26}\), giving \(\cos\theta=\frac{2 \sqrt{26}}{39}\).

Therefore \(\theta=74.8^\circ\).

sections.title: When does a zero dot product show a right angle?
sections.label: Test a right angle
sections.intro: The dot product of non-zero vectors vanishes exactly when the cosine of their angle is zero. This gives an equation for unknown components.

blocks.html: For directions \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\), use \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=0\). For two lines to meet at a right angle, also establish that they intersect.
The zero vector has zero dot product with every vector but defines no angle.

blocks.title: Use perpendicularity to find a coefficient
blocks.prompt: Find \(k\) when \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}k\\-5\\2\end{pmatrix}\) are perpendicular.

retry.feedback: The two known products add to −16. The remaining product must be +16 so that the sum is zero.

blocks.hint: A zero dot product is the condition for two non-zero perpendicular vectors.
blocks.solution:
Both vectors have non-zero length when perpendicular. Their scalar product must be zero.

The equation is \(5 k - 16=0\).

Solving gives \(k=\frac{16}{5}\).

sections.title: What does a negative projected component mean?
sections.label: Interpret projection
sections.intro: Taking the dot product with a unit direction gives the signed length of a component. A negative result means the component points against the chosen direction.

blocks.html: The signed component of \(\mathbf a\) along non-zero \(\mathbf d\) is \(\mathbf a\cdot\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\). It equals \(|\mathbf a|\cos\theta\).
A negative signed component is useful information. An actual distance is never negative.

blocks.title: Find a signed component along a direction
blocks.prompt: Find the signed scalar component of \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) along the direction \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Give an exact value.
blocks.hint: Divide by the direction's magnitude before using it in the scalar product.
blocks.solution:
Turn the direction into a unit vector \(\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{2}{3}\\\frac{2}{3}\\- \frac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\).

Take the dot product with that unit vector. The signed component is \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The angle between the two arrows with their tails placed together.

solution: Use the direction vectors. Their dot product is \(-6\). The absolute value gives the smaller angle because either direction can represent a line.
The magnitudes are \(\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{17}\), giving \(\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{102}}{17}\).

examples.question: Find \(k\) when \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\k\\7\end{pmatrix}\) are perpendicular.
solution: Both vectors have non-zero length when perpendicular. Their scalar product must be zero.
The equation is \(37 - 3 k=0\).
Solving gives \(k=\frac{37}{3}\).

examples.title: Find a signed component along a direction
examples.question: Find the signed scalar component of \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) along the direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\). Give an exact value.

orig_9709_p3_vec_line_relationships.description: Classify two lines in space, verify coordinate consistency and find an intersection when it exists.

sections.title: How can I tell if two lines are parallel?
sections.label: Compare directions
sections.intro: Check whether the second direction equals a non-zero scalar times the first. Then distinguish a single common line from two distinct parallel lines.

blocks.html: If \(\mathbf e=c\mathbf d\), test whether the difference of the anchors also equals a scalar times \(\mathbf d\). If it does, the lines are coincident.
A zero component calls for a direct comparison. Do not divide by it.

blocks.title: Classify a pair of lines
blocks.prompt: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}0\\-9\\3\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
blocks.solution:
The second direction is \(-3\) times the first. Test the displacement between anchors \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) against that direction.

The lines are distinct and parallel. Their anchor displacement is not a multiple of the direction.

sections.title: How can different equations give the same line?
sections.label: Test coincident lines
sections.intro: A point of one parallel line lies on the other precisely when the two lines coincide. Check the anchor difference to show this directly.

blocks.html: Look for two scalar relationships, one between the directions and one between the anchor displacement and a direction.
Different anchor points do not rule out coincident lines.

blocks.title: Classify a pair of lines
blocks.prompt: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\-8\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\6\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The directions are parallel. Check the difference of the anchors too: it is also a multiple of the direction, so the equations describe the same line.

blocks.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
blocks.solution:
The second direction is \(3\) times the first. Test the displacement between anchors \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\\-8\end{pmatrix}\) against that direction.

The lines are coincident. Both anchors lie on the same line and its directions are parallel.

sections.title: How do I find where two lines meet?
sections.label: Find an intersection
sections.intro: For non-parallel directions, a shared point can occur only once. Use two separate parameters, one for each line. Equate their three coordinate expressions.

blocks.html: Solve two independent coordinate equations, then verify the unused one. Substitute the parameter into either full line equation to state the intersection.
Reporting only the two parameter values does not answer a question asking for the point of intersection.

blocks.title: Classify a pair of lines
blocks.prompt: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\-5\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Give all coordinates of their intersection.
blocks.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
blocks.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(t + 4=3 u - 1\) and \(3 - t=u + 4\) to get \(t=-2\) and \(u=1\).

The remaining z-coordinates are \(-6\) and \(-6\).

All three coordinates match. The lines intersect at \((2, 5, -6)\).

sections.title: What makes two lines skew?
sections.label: Check the third equation
sections.intro: Two non-parallel lines in 3D can miss each other. If the only candidate from two independent equations fails the third, the lines are skew.

blocks.html: Skew means non-parallel and non-intersecting. Show both facts from the direction and coordinate tests.

figure.alt: A wireframe cuboid shows one horizontal front bottom edge and one vertical back edge highlighted. The edges never meet.
figure.caption: The highlighted edges lie in different faces. The blue edge is horizontal, the teal edge vertical, and their extensions have no common point.

blocks.html: An apparent crossing in a 2D drawing does not prove that the lines share the same third coordinate.

blocks.title: Classify a pair of lines
blocks.prompt: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-5\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\11\\-1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The first two coordinate equations locate a candidate. The third coordinate differs, so the lines are skew.

blocks.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
blocks.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(2 t=- u\) and \(t + 4=3 u + 11\) to get \(t=1\) and \(u=-2\).

The remaining z-coordinates are \(-4\) and \(-1\).

The third equation fails, although the directions are not parallel. The lines are skew.

sections.title: What if the first two equations depend on each other?
sections.label: Choose an equation pair
sections.intro: If solving the first two coordinate equations gives the same condition twice, use another coordinate equation. If two equations are inconsistent, there can be no intersection.

blocks.html: For non-parallel directions, some pair of coordinate equations is independent. Use that pair to determine both parameters before the final check.
A mismatch in an equation with no parameters also rules out intersection. Do not discard a fixed coordinate.

blocks.title: Classify a pair of lines
blocks.prompt: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}5\\11\\-1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\\1\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
blocks.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(t + 1=2 u + 5\) and \(2 - 2 t=u - 1\) to get \(t=2\) and \(u=-1\).

The remaining y-coordinates are \(4\) and \(5\).

The third equation fails, although the directions are not parallel. The lines are skew.

solution: Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.
The remaining z-coordinates are \(6\) and \(8\).
The third equation fails, although the directions are not parallel. The lines are skew.

The remaining y-coordinates are \(-5\) and \(-5\).
All three coordinates match. The lines intersect at \((-2, -5, -6)\).

extraPractice.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(3 t + 1=2 - u\) and \(t + 4=2 u + 9\) to get \(t=1\) and \(u=-2\).

The remaining z-coordinates are \(1\) and \(3\).

The third equation fails, although the directions are not parallel. The lines are skew.

extraPractice.hint: Test direction vectors first. If they are not proportional, solve two independent coordinate equations and check the third.
extraPractice.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(t + 5=3 u\) and \(4 t + 1=7 - u\) to get \(t=1\) and \(u=2\).

The remaining y-coordinates are \(-1\) and \(-1\).

All three coordinates match. The lines intersect at \((6, -1, 5)\).

sections.title: Where does a perpendicular from P reach a line?
sections.label: Set up the foot
sections.intro: Write the foot \(F\) as a general point on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to the line direction.

blocks.html: For \(\mathbf f=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\) and point \(P\) with position vector \(\mathbf p\), solve \((\mathbf p-\mathbf f)\cdot\mathbf d=0\).

figure.alt: A dashed perpendicular drops from P to F on line l. A different point X on the line joins P at a slant.
figure.caption: \(F\) is on the line, and \(PF\) makes a right angle with it. The route to a different point \(X\) is longer.

blocks.html: \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) is the movement from the anchor to \(P\). The perpendicular condition uses the unknown \(F\), not the anchor.

blocks.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
blocks.prompt: For \(P(5, 8, -1)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\). Give the parameter and every coordinate of \(F\).
blocks.hint: Write F as a general point on the line first. Its displacement to P has dot product zero with the direction vector.
blocks.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(15 - 14 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{15}{14}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{41}{14}, \frac{73}{14}, \frac{15}{7})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(\frac{41}{14}, \frac{73}{14}, \frac{15}{7})\) at \(t=\frac{15}{14}\).

sections.title: How do I verify a candidate perpendicular foot?
sections.label: Check both conditions
sections.intro: A foot must lie on the given line and make a right angle with it. Solve for the parameter first and substitute back into the line. Test both conditions if a point has already been proposed.

blocks.html: When \(\mathbf d\ne\mathbf 0\), the equation gives exactly one value \(t=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf d}\).
The denominator is the square of the direction’s length. A non-unit direction cannot be treated as a unit direction.

blocks.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
blocks.prompt: For \(P(5, 1, 7)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\). Give the parameter and every coordinate of \(F\).
blocks.hint: Write F as a general point on the line first. Its displacement to P has dot product zero with the direction vector.
blocks.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(10 - 9 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{10}{9}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{11}{9}, \frac{47}{9}, \frac{55}{9})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(\frac{11}{9}, \frac{47}{9}, \frac{55}{9})\) at \(t=\frac{10}{9}\).

sections.title: Why is the perpendicular the shortest route?
sections.label: Measure the distance
sections.intro: For any other point \(X\) on the line, triangle \(PFX\) is right-angled at \(F\). So \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\), and any non-zero \(FX\) increases the distance.

blocks.html: After locating \(F\), the point-to-line distance is \(|\mathbf p-\mathbf f|\). If \(P\) already lies on the line, the foot is \(P\) and the distance is zero.
Distance to a chosen anchor is generally longer than distance to the line. Calculate the foot first.

blocks.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
blocks.prompt: For \(P(2, 7, -1)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\) and exact distance \(PF\). Give every coordinate of \(F\).
blocks.hint: Write F as a general point on the line first. Its displacement to P has dot product zero with the direction vector.
blocks.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(- 11 t=0\), so \(t=0\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(0, 3, 1)\).

The foot is \(F(0, 3, 1)\) and \(PF=2 \sqrt{6}\). Use the magnitude of the perpendicular displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: How does the method work with a solid?
sections.label: Use the geometry
sections.intro: Assign axes along mutually perpendicular edges. For a cuboid, the coordinates of each vertex can then be read from its side lengths. Build the line and perpendicular condition from these coordinates.

blocks.html: Choose a clear origin and keep the same coordinate order throughout. Use the full spatial direction of the edge or diagonal in the dot product.
A diagram flattens depth. A visual right angle is only a cue, while the dot product verifies the calculation.

blocks.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
blocks.prompt: For \(P(3, 0, 4)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\) and exact distance \(PF\). Give every coordinate of \(F\).
blocks.hint: Write F as a general point on the line first. Its displacement to P has dot product zero with the direction vector.
blocks.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(25 - 41 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{25}{41}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{75}{41}, \frac{100}{41}, \frac{100}{41})\).

The foot is \(F(\frac{75}{41}, \frac{100}{41}, \frac{100}{41})\) and \(PF=\frac{20 \sqrt{41}}{41}\). Use the magnitude of the perpendicular displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{48}{41}\\- \frac{100}{41}\\\frac{64}{41}\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: When does the nearest point on a segment lie at an endpoint?
sections.label: Check the parameter interval
sections.intro: For application questions on a finite segment, use the closest point on its supporting line first. If the foot lies outside the segment, compare the endpoints or use \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\) to choose the closer endpoint.

blocks.html: If \(\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+t\overrightarrow{AB}\), a foot with \(0\le t\le1\) lies on segment \(AB\).
Do not report a foot outside the segment as a point of that segment.

blocks.title: Find the nearest point on a closed segment
blocks.prompt: Find the point of segment \(AB\) nearest to \(P(-3, 0, 0)\). \(A(0, 0, 2)\) and \(B(2, 3, 3)\). Give all coordinates and the exact distance.

retry.feedback: That x-coordinate belongs to the foot on the supporting line. Its parameter is outside the segment, so the nearest point on the segment is A.

blocks.hint: Find the perpendicular foot on the whole line, then compare its parameter to the endpoint parameters.
blocks.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(- 14 t - 8=0\), so \(t=- \frac{4}{7}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(- \frac{8}{7}, - \frac{12}{7}, \frac{10}{7})\).

The foot parameter \(- \frac{4}{7}\) is outside \([0,1]\). The nearest allowable parameter is \(0\).

The nearest point is \((0, 0, 2)\) and its distance from \(P\) is \(\sqrt{13}\).

glossary.definition: The point on a line reached by a perpendicular from a given point.
The length from the point to its perpendicular foot.
The full straight line containing a given segment.

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
examples.question: For \(P(-1, 9, -5)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\) and exact distance \(PF\). Give every coordinate of \(F\).

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(144 - 169 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{144}{169}\).
Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{576}{169}, \frac{432}{169}, \frac{1728}{169})\).

The foot is \(F(\frac{576}{169}, \frac{432}{169}, \frac{1728}{169})\) and \(PF=\frac{60}{13}\). Use the magnitude of the perpendicular displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{576}{169}\\- \frac{432}{169}\\\frac{300}{169}\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find the nearest point on a closed segment
examples.question: Find the point of segment \(AB\) nearest to \(P(4, 2, 4)\). \(A(2, 0, 1)\) and \(B(4, 1, 3)\). Give all coordinates and the exact distance.
solution: Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.
Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(12 - 9 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{4}{3}\).

The foot parameter \(\frac{4}{3}\) is outside \([0,1]\). The nearest allowable parameter is \(1\).
The nearest point is \((4, 1, 3)\) and its distance from \(P\) is \(\sqrt{2}\).
